title: Evaluating the potential impacts of solar farms on hydrological responses
abstract: With the demand for green energy rapidly increasing, solar energy as a renewable energy source is expanding across the world. Implementing solar energy on a large scale requires solar farm installation on land covering hundreds of acres of area. Solar farms also change the existing land use and affect the hydrological response of the catchment. However, the impact of solar farms on catchment hydrology is not well understood, in part due to the lack of established modelling methods tailored to their unique land cover. The areas over which solar panels are installed are impervious on the panel and pervious underneath it, making it challenging to model. In this study, a framework is proposed to model the hydrological response of a solar farm using EPA SWMM. The framework split each row of the solar farm into four sections, the impervious solar panel, a wet section at the dripline that captures the majority of runoff from the panel, a spacer section that encompasses the space between the solar panel rows, and an under-panel section which represents the space under the solar panel. The runoff from one section is routed to the next section in the order of natural water flow. All these sections represent one row of the solar farm, so the runoff from each row is then routed to the next row until the outlet. With this general setup, many variables such as land cover, the slope of land and solar panel, panel width, rainfall events can be easily modified to understand the effect on hydrology for specific scenarios. This relatively simple framework can improve our ability to represent the hydrological response of a catchment before and after the installation of solar farms and can serve as preliminary tool for planning purpose.

## **Evaluating the potential impacts of solar farms on hydrological responses**

## **Nair, Adira Ajith[1] ., A.N Rohith[1 .] , Raj, Cibin[1,2] ., Lauren E McPhillips[1,2] .**

1Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA 16802

2Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA 16802

## **Written for presentation at the 2022 ASABE Annual International Meeting Sponsored by ASABE Houston, Texas July 17–20, 2022**

**ABSTRACT.** _With the demand for green energy rapidly increasing, solar energy as a renewable energy source is expanding across the world. Implementing solar energy on a large scale requires solar farm installation on land covering hundreds of acres of area. Solar farms also change the existing land use and affect the hydrological response of the catchment. However, the impact of solar farms on catchment hydrology is not well understood, in part due to the lack of established modelling methods tailored to their unique land cover. The areas over which solar panels are installed are impervious on the panel and pervious underneath it, making it challenging to model. In this study, a framework is proposed to model the hydrological response of a solar farm using EPA SWMM. The framework split each row of the solar farm into four sections, the impervious solar panel, a wet section at the dripline that captures the majority of runoff from the panel, a spacer section that encompasses the space between the solar panel rows, and an under-panel section which represents the space under the solar panel. The runoff from one section is routed to the next section in the order of natural water flow. All these sections represent one row of the solar farm, so the runoff from each row is then routed to the next row until the outlet. With this general setup, many variables such as land cover, the slope of land and solar panel, panel width, rainfall events can be easily modified to understand the effect on hydrology for specific scenarios. This relatively simple framework can improve our ability to represent the hydrological response of a catchment before and after the installation of solar farms and can serve as preliminary tool for planning purpose._

_**Keywords.** Solar farms, SWMM, hydrology, land-use change_

## **1. Introduction**

The rising energy demands since the industrial revolution have contributed significantly to global warming. The United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (2018) estimates that the energy sector accounts for around 60% of the total greenhouse gas emissions. It is also highlighted in the Global Energy Outlook (2022) that the projected increase in energy demand by the year 2050 compared to 2020 is around 53%. In this light, deploying renewable and affordable energy resources such as solar is vital for mitigating climate change impacts. Among renewable energy resources, solar energy is preferred due to its abundance and affordability. The utilization of solar energy is becoming increasingly cheaper due to technological development and government policies; also, the cost of photovoltaics used in solar farms is expected to reduce by 60% by 2030 (Solar Futures Study, 2021). A study by the U.S Department of Energy (2021) suggests that solar energy could account for nearly 40% of the nation’s electricity supply by 2035 and 45% by 2050.

Solar energy is harvested in numerous ways, among which arrays of ground-mounted solar panel installations with a capacity of at least 1 megawatt, referred to as solar farms, are typical (U. S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review, 2022)). Solar energy is also one of the sources with minimal environmental impacts in terms of solid waste, ground contamination, biodiversity, and water quality; however, the adverse land-use effects can vary depending upon the location and nature of installations (Aman et al., 2015). A solar farm requires ample installation space and could alter the biophysical characteristics, land use, land cover, and agricultural capacity of the watershed (Hernandez et al., 2019). The landscape modification in the process of solar farm construction could modify the soil properties and vegetation (Choi et al., 2020; Lambert et al., 2021). The process of solar farm construction could disturb the topsoil and alter vegetation and may accelerate the erosion of fine particles by water (Hernandez et al., 2014). Adding impervious solar panels could alter the catchment hydrological behaviour and change the runoff hydrograph shapes. However, there is currently very limited field observations of any hydrological changes resulting from solar farm implementation and how this may vary based on site selection and management practices (Yavari Bajehbaj et al., 2022).

There has been some limited investigation of the implications of solar farms on landscape hydrology using hydrological models (Yavari Bajehbaj et al., 2022). Edalat (2017) reported that the installation of solar panels significantly increased the volume of the peak runoff from the catchment. A higher volume of runoff was observed for smaller panel tilt angles due to the larger surface area of the panel, and higher peak flows were observed for panel tilt angles close to zero and orientation angles between 90° and 225° to the ground slope. In a catchment scale study using the Soil and Water Assessment Tool to model a portion of the catchment as solar panel covered, Pisinaras et al. (2014) reported an increase in surface runoff of around 150 mm at the subbasin scale. Pisinaras et al. (2014) also reported an increase in infiltration and a decrease in evapotranspiration. However, one of the limitations of these studies was that the solar panel area was modelled only once, which may not be accurate for ground-mounted panels, where flow and infiltration can also occur under the panel. Cook and McCuen (2013) custom-built a model to represent the hydrologic behaviour of both the panel area and under the panel area and studied multiple scenarios of solar farm construction. They observed a significant increase in the runoff volume and around a 100% increase in peak runoff in a scenario where land cover is altered after solar farm construction. However, if the area goes through minimal land changes, the increase in volume and peak of runoff may not be significant enough to implement stormwater management strategies (Cook & McCuen, 2013). Also, numerous field-based studies around the globe (Choi et al., 2020; Lambert et al., 2021; Tanner et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2021) evaluated the effect of solar farm construction on soil quality, surface moisture conditions, microclimate, vegetation, evapotranspiration and temperature. While solar panels may alter some soil and hydrological properties, there are opportunities to implement management practices to manage any adverse impacts; thus, it is critical to have hydrological models that can accurately represent the unique conditions of solar farms.

Most of the studies discussed above either use more complex data-intensive models or lack sufficient conceptual representation of the solar farm in the model. In this study, an attempt is made to use the United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) to model the hydrological response of the solar farm. SWMM is simple yet sufficiently represents the physics to model hydrology and hydraulics and has been widely used for various planning and design purposes. A solar farm hydrology modelling framework developed using SWMM would help managers who are already accustomed to using SWMM to leverage it for solar farm stormwater management planning.

## **2. Study area and data**

A solar farm site in State College, Pennsylvania, was used as a reference to generate model representations of a solar farm. One of the reasons for selecting this site was its high site slope which is 23%, while the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (Chapter 102 Permitting for solar panel farms, 2021) recommends the site slope for solar farms to be less than 10% and up to 15% under certain conditions. The section of the solar farm used to create the SWMM model is highlighted in Figure 1 using a yellow box. The solar panel length, spacer length, site slope, and solar panel width were measured manually using a tape measure. The soil data were obtained from the USDA NRCS Web Soil Survey (https://websoilsurvey.sc.egov.usda.gov/App/WebSoilSurvey.aspx). Rainfall data required for the analysis was downloaded

from the NOAA (https://hdsc.nws.noaa.gov/hdsc/pfds/) data archive for State College, PA. The solar form and catchment characteristics are presented in Table 1.

**Figure 1. Aerial view of the study area.**

## **3. Methodology**

## **Model configuration**

A solar farm generally consists of solar panels installed in rows separated by equal spacing. For modelling, each solar panel cell was divided into four components as shown in the schematic in Figure 2 (a, b), (i) panel, (ii) under-panel, (iii) wet zone, and (iv) spacer. The surface of the solar panel on which the rain falls directly is a panel. These panels are mounted above the ground with metal supports, and the ground area below the panels is called the under panel. The wet zone is where the rainwater flows directly from a panel edge, and a spacer is the remaining interspace area between rows of solar panels (Fig 2). All the sections except the under-panel receive water from the rainfall, and the wet zone receives water directly from the panel along with rainfall. Among an under-panel, a wet zone, and a spacer section, water can move from one to any other zone depending on the ground slope, as shown in Figure 2 (a, b). For a better understanding of the nature of the flow, two cases of ground slope corresponding to the slope of the panels were considered, case-1: both solar panels and the ground have the same slope direction, and case-2: both solar panels and the ground have the opposite slope direction. In case 1, water flows from the wet zone to the spacer of the same cell and from the spacer to the under-panel of the downstream cell and then to the next wet zone. In case 2, the water flows from the wet section to the under-panel of the same cell and underpanel to the spacer of the downstream cell and continues to the next wet section.

**Figure 2. Schematic representing two cases of solar panel placement.**

## **SWMM model setup.**

An EPA SWMM model was set up with the above conceptualization of the solar farms to simulate the hydrological response of the catchment. Each of the four sections in a single row was modelled as individual sub-catchments. Considering the schematic in Figure 2, all the runoff from the panel was routed to the wet section irrespective of the two slope direction cases (panel 1 to wet 1, panel 2 to wet 2, and panel 3 to wet 3). The runoff from wet 1, 2 and 3 was routed to spacer 1, 2, and 3, respectively, in case-1, and to under-panel 1, 2, and 3, respectively, in case-2. In case-1, the flow from spacer 1 and 2 were routed to downstream row under-panel 2 and 3, respectively. In case-2, the flow from under-panel 2 and 3 was routed to downstream row spacer 1 and 2, respectively.

Further, SWMM assumes the flow to be sheet flow (overland flow) within the sub-catchments. However, when an entire solar farm with multiple rows is considered, sheet flow may not prevail at all the downstream rows due to the limiting length of the sheet flow. Based on the recommendations from NRCS National Engineering Handbook Part 630 Hydrology (Chapter 15: Time of Concentration), a maximum of 100ft was assumed as sheet flow length for this study.

The total width of a single solar farm panel row is 23.8 ft (solar panel, wet section, spacer); therefore, the flow was assumed to be sheet flow until four rows of panels are modelled as flow from sub-catchments. Any flow after four-panel rows were assumed to be shallow concentrated flows and were modelled as grass-lined, parabolic open channel concentrated flows with a channel width of 1ft. Considering a 10-row solar panel array, junctions J1, J2, and J3 were created at the end of the 4[th] , 8[th] and 10[th] rows, respectively. The flow from the first four panel arrays was drained to J1 and the flow from next four to J2 and the flow form last two to J3. Junctions J1, J2, and J3 were connected through conduits C1 and C2 to facilitate shallow concentrated flow towards downstream. The flow in J3 was drained to an outfall through conduit C3. The site slope of 23% was utilized for calculating the invert elevation of the conduits. The SWMM model setup is presented in Figure 3.

**Figure 3. SWMM model setup for 10 rows of solar panel arrays.**

## **4. Results and discussions**

## **Panel slope in the direction of the watershed (Current conditions).**

A 24-hour 100 return period storm was used to simulate the hydrological response of the solar farm in the existing conditions to understand the infiltration and runoff patterns in the various sections of the solar farm arrays. The simulation results are presented in Figure 4. The inflow depth to the wet area of all the rows is large until it reaches junction after the 4[th] , 8[th] and 10[th] rows, compared to other sections as wet sections surface area is low due to 1ft width assumption. Also, all the rainfall that impervious solar panel receives flow into the wet section without any infiltration. Since the wet section receives a high inflow in a short span, it generates more runoff by both meeting the infiltration demand and exceeding the infiltration capacity of the soil, as shown in Figure 4. The water from the panel to the wet section may have kinetic energy up to 10 times that of rainfall (Cook & McCuen, 2013) and may lead to significant soil erosion. Hence, implementation of management practices such as infiltration trenches or stone drip beds in the wet area could reduce the runoff by increasing the infiltration and also could reduce soil erosion (Yavari Bajehbaj et al., 2022).

**Figure 4. Total inflow, Runoff, and Infiltration at all the sub-catchments of the study area for a 24-hour, 100-year design storm.**

Further, the runoff hydrographs of the sub-catchments for the fourth row are plotted in Figure 5, and the remaining rows have a similar pattern. The wet and the spacer sub-catchments of Row-4 were observed to have two peaks. The initial peak is due to the high-intensity rainfall between 11[th] and 12[th] hours (midpoint of the 24-hour storm) of the simulation. Also, the first peak was recorded at the sub-catchments of all the rows except under-panels, as they do not receive direct rainfall. The second peak is mainly due to the excess runoff from the upstream sub-catchments, and the solar panel is the only subcatchment that does not experience the second peak, as it does not receive any upstream runoff. The hydrograph of the spacer sub-catchment was observed to be the largest of all, as it is the downstream sub-catchment of the solar panel row for panels with a slope direction the same as the site slope direction.

**Figure 5. Runoff hydrographs (left) and infiltration rates (right) from sub-catchments of the fourth row of the solar farm for a 24-hour, 100year design storm when solar panels and site slope are in the same direction.**

In addition to analyzing the runoff behaviour of sub-catchments, the pattern of infiltration in various sub-catchments was also studied, and the graphs for the fourth row are presented in Figure 5. Wet section infiltration followed the ideal exponential decay as the inflow rate was higher than the infiltration capacity due to the high inflow from the solar panel. The wet sections also had the lowest width (1 ft), which saturated quickly, making the infiltration rate reach a steady state early (around 10 h). The spacer section may have saturated at around 6 h and reached the steady state infiltration. The underpanel section might not have completely saturated until 16 h as the infiltration rate seems exponentially decay only after 16h, and the power decay from 12h to 16h might have been due to a decrease in the rainfall intensity after 12h.

## **Panel slope in the opposite direction to watershed**

The slope direction of the solar panel can be in the same direction as the site slope or in the opposite direction, depending on the site location. The change in the slope direction changes the chronology of the flow from one sub-catchment to another, as demonstrated in Section 3 (Figure 2b). An SWMM model was set up to represent the condition when the solar panel direction is opposite to the direction of slope, and catchment response was simulated for 24h, 100y return period design storm. The model with both panel and site slope in the same direction is referred to as Case-1, and the other as Case-2. The surface runoff hydrograph for the fourth solar panel row for case-2 is plotted in Figure 6. Unlike case-1 where both spacer and wet sections had two peaks towards row-4, in case-2 only the wet section had two peaks. In case-2 as the water flows from the wet section to the under-panel first and then to the spacer section, infiltration in the under-panel might have reduced the flow into the spacer section and thereby curtailing the first peak as well as the runoff magnitude throughout the simulation period for the spacer section. It can also be noted from Figure 6 that more under-panel infiltration starts from the beginning of the rainfall itself due to high runoff from the wet area. Also, since the under-panel does not receive any rainfall, all its infiltration needs to be met by the runoff itself.

**Figure 6. Runoff hydrographs (left) and infiltration rates (right) from sub-catchments of the fourth row of the solar farm for a 24-hour, 100year design storm when solar panels and site slope are in the opposite direction.**

Further, in a comparison of the total catchment outflow, Case-2, where both panels and site slope are in the opposite direction, was observed to have a high runoff volume (77000 gal) compared to case-1, where it was 74000 gal; however, the

peak runoff (1.68 CFS) in case-1  was lower and earlier than that of case-2. The higher peak in case-1 can be attributed to high rainfall intensity around the 12[th] hour of rainfall, while the effect of high rainfall intensity might have diminished due to high infiltration in the under-panel section in case-2.

## **Pre and post-solar farm development comparison**

An analysis of the hydrological response of the catchments pre and post-solar farm construction is vital for implementing stormwater management strategies. For this purpose, the current condition model used in the above section was taken for the post-solar farm construction scenario. For the pre-solar farm construction condition, the solar panel sub-catchments were removed, and the rain gauge with rainfall was connected to the under-panel sub-catchment. Both the pre and post-solar farms construction SWMM models were run for a  24 h duration, and 2-y, 10-y, 25-y, 50-y, and 100-y return period design storms. The results for outfall volume and maximum flow are tabulated in Table 2 and Table 3.

**Table 2: Maximum flow and Outfall volume for 24-hours storms for pre and post-solar farms construction** .

||**Post**|**Pre**|**Post**|**Pre**|

It was observed that the construction of solar farms led to an additional 11,000 (14.5%) gallons of runoff in the catchment for a 100 y, 24 h design storm. The peak flow rate after post-solar farm construction was consistently higher than the precondition for all the return period events.

## **Limitations and future suggestions**

The EPA SWMM tool is simple and flexible to model the solar farm hydrology; however, the flow was modelled as 1- dimensional, which may not accurately represent reality. Assumptions such as 1-foot top width and parabolic shape were made for channel flows, which may require field measurements to gain confidence in the simulation results. Similarly, the soil properties such as the suction head and conductivity were obtained through the NRCS Soil Survey, but the model would have been more accurate if these were field measurements. Further, the SWMM model used in this study was uncalibrated due to the limitations of available flow measurements; efforts are ongoing to collect field data to be able to validate and improve future modelling representations of solar farms.

## **5. Conclusions**

In this study, a framework was proposed to model the hydrological response of a solar farm using EPA SWMM. This approach builds upon existing work by leveraging a well known stormwater model to improve the representation of this unique land use. The framework splits each row of the solar farm into four sections, the impervious solar panel, a wet section that captures the majority of runoff from the panel, a spacer section that encompasses the space between the solar panel rows after the wet section, and an under-panel section which represents the space under the solar panel. The runoff from one section was routed to the next section in the order of natural water flow. All these sections represent one row of the solar farm, such that the runoff from each row is then routed to the next row until the outlet. A comparison of model simulations from solar panel slope in the same direction as site slope was observed to have a lower peak runoff rate compared to the case with solar panel row in the opposite direction of the site slope.

Further, in comparison with the pre solar farm construction scenario, it was noted that the construction of solar farms would increase both peak runoff and total volume of runoff. Further validation and model development is necessary, but this framework is an important step toward improving the representation of solar farms in hydrological modelling. We hope this approach can be leveraged to study the hydrological response of the catchment before and after the installation of solar farms and to improve the evaluation of runoff and suitable stormwater management strategies, facilitating sustainable development of this critical renewable energy strategy
